2.text: Whaling was done in former times chiefly by the Arctic Chukchee, and

3.text: on the Pacific coast by the Eskimo. For this purpose a large harpoon, with

4.text: a heavy head perforated at right angles to the blade, was used.
4.note: Composite showed a faint raised mark after 'blade,'; at 2x zoom it resolves as show-through from the line above's descenders, not ink of this line. No mark keyed.

5.text: The line was very long and stout, and floats were attached

6.text: to it in pairs at several places. Altogether there were two,

7.text: three, or even four pairs. Now, on the Pacific, but little

8.text: whaling is done, and that exclusively by the Eskimo of Indian

9.text: Point, of Cape Chukotsky, of Cape Ulakhpen, and also by
9.note: Composite showed apparent marks near 'Cape'/'Ulakhpen'; at 2x these resolve as show-through from the line above, not diacritics. Ulakhpen has a plain capital U.

10.text: the inhabitants of Čibuˊkak on St. Lawrence Island. They
10.resolved: Č = C+U+030C; ˊ = U+02CA stress after u

11.text: all use explosive harpoons. On the Arctic the number of

12.text: whales has also considerably dwindled. Thus the natives of

13.text: Yaˊqan told Maydell that they had hardly caught a whale in

14.text: later years. The whalers ceased going along the Arctic shore

15.text: of Asia, because whales became too scarce in that region.

16.text: The single harpoon-head that I was able to procure at Indian

17.text: Point is old and worn, showing that it is the remains of an

18.text: old, now unused weapon (Fig. 42, a, b).
18.note: Machine draft read '6' for the italic figure-part locant; at 2x zoom it is clearly an italic letter b, matching the 'a,' before it.

19.text: The white whale is killed in the same way as the walrus,

20.text: with the rifle, and sometimes with the harpoon. The natives

21.text: eagerly pursue it, because its meat and blubber taste better than

22.text: those of any other sea-animal (Plates X, Fig. 4; XI, Fig. 1).
22.note: Plate numbers are printed as lowercase roman numerals ('x', 'xi'); keyed as plain ASCII capitals per keying_spec.md §2.12 ('Every roman numeral in the book is keyed in plain ASCII capitals, whatever the setting').

23.text: I did not find current among the Chukchee the notion, peculiar
23.note: Composite showed an apparent mark over 'notion'; at 2x it resolves as show-through from the line above.

24.text: to some American Eskimo, that white whales must be struck

25.text: with a flint.¹ It is curious that this idea re-appears among the
25.note: Footnote reference marker, printed as a raised digit; machine draft substituted '!'. Keyed as U+00B9 per §2.10.

26.text: Koryak on the Okhotsk Sea, in the villages of Kamenskoye

28.text: SEALING-NETS. — Sealing-nets are perhaps still more efficient

29.text: than harpoons, especially in the winter-time. They are made

30.text: of thin strips of seal-skin or reindeer-skin, with buoys of wood

31.text: or of inflated pieces of gut, and stone or ivory sinkers. A

32.text: peculiar net used on the Arctic and on portions of the Pacific

33.text: coast is square in shape, and is fastened beneath the seal’s

34.text: breathing-hole like a cradle (Fig. 43, a).² For this purpose
34.note: Footnote reference marker, printed as a raised digit '2'. Keyed as U+00B2 per §2.10.

35.text: four wooden poles tied to the mouth of the net are put through

36.text: the hole and arranged underneath the ice so as to form a

37.text: square. The net hangs by the corners on short cords, allowing

38.text: the seal a free passage into the hole from all sides. The seal,

39.text: arriving at the hole, may see perfectly well that something

40.text: unusual has happened, but, as it is its breathing-time, it slips in between the

41.text: net and the ice, and rises to the surface. That done, it will, as is its wont,
